Black Death Accusations

1348: the well-poisoning charge, the confessions, and the Pope's letters saying it was false.

3 note files

The Plague Comes to Europe

In 1347 a sickness out of Asia reached the ports of Sicily and Italy, and by 1348 it was in France, Spain, England, and the German lands. It was plague — carried, though no one then knew it, by the fleas of rats — and it killed on a scale Europe had never seen. Modern historians put the dead at between thirty and sixty of every hundred people in Europe; the highest modern estimate counts some fifty million dead. Town after town buried a third to a half of its people in a single season.

Source: “Black Death” — Wikipedia

The Charge: Poison in the Wells

As the dying spread, a story spread with it: the Jews had done it, by poisoning the wells and springs of Christendom in a single great plot. In September 1348, at the Castle of Chillon on Lake Geneva, the story was given the shape of proof. A Jewish surgeon named Balavignus was put on the rack until he confessed that a rabbi of Toledo had sent him poison in a stitched leather bag, to throw into the wells. Others were tortured into matching confessions — Agimet of Geneva, at Châtel, on October 20, 1348, among them. The written confessions were then copied and sent from town to town down the Rhine, arriving in each city as official evidence — before the plague itself arrived.

Source: The Black Death accusations — primary texts (CCJR, Boston College)

The Burnings

The killing began at Toulon in April 1348 and ran ahead of the disease. At Basel in January 1349 the Jews were burned in a wooden house built on an island in the Rhine, and the city swore to admit no Jew for two hundred years. At Speyer the dead were packed in wine casks and thrown into the river. At Strasbourg the council that had protected the Jews was overthrown by the guilds, and on February 14, 1349 — before the plague had even reached the city — about two thousand Jews were burned on a platform in their own cemetery, as the city chronicler Königshofen records. Worms, Erfurt, Frankfurt, Mainz, and Cologne followed through 1349; at Mainz the Jews fought back before they were overwhelmed. At Nuremberg in December the council had arranged the killing two months ahead and divided the property in advance.

Source: The Black Death accusations — primary texts (CCJR, Boston College)

The Pope’s Answer

One great authority said, in writing, that the charge was false. Pope Clement VI, at Avignon, issued a bull on July 6, 1348 renewing the Church's old protection of the Jews, and on September 26, 1348 a second bull against the accusation itself: “certain Christians, seduced by that liar, the devil, are imputing the pestilence to poisoning by Jews.” His reasons were plain facts — Jews were dying of the plague in the same proportions as Christians, and the plague raged in places where no Jews lived at all. He forbade the killing and the forced baptisms on pain of excommunication, and in his own city of Avignon the Jews were kept safe. Strasbourg's first council, Cologne's council, and the citizens of Regensburg also tried to protect their Jews. The Emperor Charles IV went the other way, letting the killers keep what they seized.

Source: “Black Death Jewish persecutions” — Wikipedia

The Money Underneath

Strasbourg's own chronicler wrote down the motive no one else would print. After the burning of February 14, 1349, every debt owed to the Jews was cancelled, their pledges surrendered, and their cash divided among the working men of the city. “The money was indeed the thing that killed the Jews,” Königshofen wrote. “If they had been poor and if the feudal lords had not been in debt to them, they would not have been burnt.” Modern Bavarian scholarship, reviewing the same records, reaches the same conclusion: the toleration and the murder of the Jews were motivated above all economically.

Source: “Judenverfolgungen (Spätmittelalter)” — Historisches Lexikon Bayerns

What Was Left

By 1351, hundreds of Jewish communities had ceased to exist — at least two hundred towns by the chroniclers' own record, and modern counts of destroyed communities run to five hundred and ten. Basel barred Jews for two hundred years. Churches rose on synagogue ground. The survivors moved east, into Poland, where King Casimir III kept his protection over them — and the centre of Jewish life in Europe moved east with them, for five hundred years. The charge itself was older than the plague: Jews had been accused of murdering children since 1144 and of torturing the consecrated host since the 1200s, and of poisoning wells once before, in France in 1321. The plague gave the old accusation a continent to burn.

Source: “Black Death Jewish persecutions” — Wikipedia

In their own words — key quotations

"And everything that was owed to the Jews was cancelled, and the Jews had to surrender all pledges and notes that they had taken for debts. The council, however, took the direct cash that the Jews possessed and divided it among the working men proportionately. The money was indeed the thing that killed the Jews. If they had been poor and if the feudal lords had not been in debt to them, they would not have been burnt."

— from: The Black Death Accusations Against the Jews, 1348–1351

"Die Pest wütete 1348 erstmals in Europa und brachte für mindestens ein Drittel der Bevölkerung den Tod. Die bakteriellen Erreger der Krankheit wie auch deren Verbreitung über die Flöhe der Ratten waren unbekannt. Schnell entstand der Vorwurf, Juden hätten, als Feinde der Christen, Wasser und Brunnen vergiftet. So eilte bald der Krankheit eine fast alle jüdischen Gemeinden betreffende Verfolgungswelle voraus."

— from: From the Bavarian State Library (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich)

"In allen schwäbischen und fränkischen Städten, in denen nach den Verfolgungen von 1336 und 1338 wieder Juden lebten, kam es zu Verfolgungen, so auch in Augsburg, wo bereits am 22. November 1348 über 100 Juden ermordet worden waren, und am 21. April 1349 in Würzburg."

— from: From the Bavarian State Library (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich)

"Die Morde an der Nürnberger Gemeinde, bei der vermutlich 562 Menschen starben, erfolgten am 6. Dezember 1349. Der Nürnberger Rat unter Führung des Patriziers Ulrich Stromer (gest. 1385) hatte bereits zwei Monate vor dem Pogrom bei Kaiser Karl IV. (reg. 1346-1378) dessen Erlaubnis als Schutzherr der jüdischen Gemeinde eingeholt. In der berühmten Markturkunde wurde bestimmt, die unmittelbar am Rathaus gelegene jüdische Siedlung abzureißen, um hier den Hauptmarkt zu errichten und an Stelle der Synagoge die heutige katholische Pfarrkirche 'Unserer lieben Frau' zu erbauen."

— from: From the Bavarian State Library (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich)

"Auch die Verteilung des jüdischen Besitzes und Außenstände wurden in Nürnberg bereits im Vorfeld geregelt. Ulrich Stromer wurde 'um seiner Treue und Dienste willen' als Anführer des Rates ein jüdisches Haus geschenkt. Der jüdische Besitz und auch die Forderungen der Juden fielen an die Stadt. Nürnberger Bürgern wurden die Schulden bei den jüdischen Gläubigern erlassen und der Bamberger Bischof und der Burggraf mit Hausschenkungen wurden mit höheren Geldsummen beteiligt."

— from: From the Bavarian State Library (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich)
